learn.title: Turning source into a program
learn.body: To run hello.c you use a terminal and a compiler. Common compilers are `clang` and `gcc`. Most systems also give you the short name `cc`. A compiler checks your code and, if it is valid, writes a runnable file.

learn.title: Compile and run
learn.body: Type these two lines in the terminal, in the folder with hello.c.

learn.title: Reading the command
learn.body: `clang` is the compiler. `hello.c` is the file to compile. `-o hello` means name the result `hello`. Without `-o`, the program is usually called `a.out`. The `./` means run the file from this folder.

learn.title: Ask for warnings
learn.body: Add `-std=c11 -Wall -Wextra` to see more helpful warnings and to use the C11 standard. Warnings are not errors, but they often point at real bugs, so read them.

learn.title: Changing the program
learn.body: Say you edit hello.c to print something else.
steps: Save the file in your editor
Run `./hello` to see the new output

learn.body: The old program does not change by itself. After every edit, compile again before you run.

questions.prompt: The `-o` flag sets the \_\_ of the compiled program.
questions.explanation: `-o hello` names the output file hello.

questions.prompt: If you leave out `-o`, the program is usually named \_\_.
Which flag turns on extra warnings? Type it, including the dash.
questions.explanation: `-Wall` turns on a large set of useful warnings. `-Wextra` adds more.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order after editing your code.
questions.explanation: You must recompile after a change, otherwise you run the old version.

questions.prompt: You change hello.c and run `./hello` without compiling. What do you see?
choices: The output of the old version
questions.explanation: The program file only changes when you compile again.
